name: Carnosic acid

card.summary: A rosemary and sage antioxidant used as a preservative in products and studied for UV and inflammation effects relevant to skin.
card.note: Most published work is laboratory or animal research.

quick.overview:
Carnosic acid is a phenolic diterpene found in rosemary and common sage, about 1.5 to 2.5% of dried leaf. It is used as an antioxidant preservative in foods and non-food products, labelled as extracts of rosemary (E392).
Its appeal in skincare is antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity that might protect skin from UV stress and help products stay stable. A randomized trial of a sage extract rich in carnosol and carnosic acid examined its effect on UV-induced redness.
quick.how: People meet it mainly as an ingredient in rosemary-extract skincare and food products rather than as a standalone item. The UV erythema trial applied an extract to test areas on the back before irradiation.
quick.risks: As with plant extracts generally, topical reactions are possible, and most research on the isolated compound is preclinical.

chain: Carnosic acid acts as an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory
Applied in rosemary or sage extracts to skin
Less UV-related redness and better-preserved skin
angle.text: Rosemary-based skincare uses carnosic acid for its antioxidant properties. Human data come from an extract trial on UV erythema.

lead: Carnosic acid (C20H28O4) is a phenolic diterpene found in rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis) and common sage (Salvia officinalis); Wikipedia puts the content of dried leaves at about 1.5 to 2.5 percent [1]. It and its derivative carnosol are used as antioxidant preservatives in foods and non-food products, listed on labels as extracts of rosemary, E392 [1]. It is the compound that gives rosemary extract much of its ability to slow the oxidation of fats and oils, which is why it turns up in both food and cosmetic formulations.

In skincare, its appeal is antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity that is meant to help protect skin from ultraviolet stress, keep formulas from going rancid, and support a calmer, healthier-looking complexion. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 40 healthy volunteers, a sage extract rich in carnosol and carnosic acid was tested on skin areas irradiated with UV light in the UV erythema test [2]. Grokipedia says cosmetic formulations such as anti-aging creams and sunscreens commonly include it at roughly 0.5 to 2 percent and links it to oxidative-stress protection of skin lipids, but names no clinical photoprotection trials for the pure compound [3].

Beyond skin, laboratory papers describe effects on inflammatory signalling, insulin resistance in muscle cells and adipocytes, and neuronal cell models [4][5][9]. A 2025 Thieme review is described in Grokipedia as linking it to dermal papilla cell proliferation in hair-loss research [3].

paras: Carnosic acid has a molar mass of about 332 g/mol, a melting point of 185 to 190 degrees Celsius, and the systematic name 11,12-dihydroxyabieta-8,11,13-trien-20-oic acid; carnosol is a derivative formed when it oxidizes [1][3]. Its catechol group is the chemical feature that lets it donate hydrogen and neutralise radicals [3].

Grokipedia describes biosynthesis in plant plastids from geranylgeranyl diphosphate via miltiradiene and a series of cytochrome P450 oxidations, with engineered yeast reaching about 35 mg/L, and says levels in rosemary rise in young leaves and glandular trichomes and fall in summer heat [3]. A 2015 Phytochemistry review is the standard overview of the compound [7].

Carnosic acid and carnosol serve as natural antioxidant preservatives in food and non-food products, appearing on ingredient lists as rosemary extract or E392 [1]. A 1992 paper by Schwarz and Ternes on antioxidative constituents of rosemary and sage is among the references cited by Wikipedia for this use [1].

Cosmetic formulations use rosemary-derived antioxidants to stabilise oils and to add antioxidant activity to creams and sun-care products [3]. The supporting rationale is that the catechol group scavenges singlet oxygen, superoxide and hydroxyl radicals, protects membranes from lipid peroxidation, and activates the Nrf2 pathway, raising the cell's own antioxidant enzymes such as HO-1 and NQO1, per Grokipedia [3]. People who use rosemary extract skincare do so with the aim of reducing UV-related redness and oxidative ageing, though the human data for the isolated compound are limited.

The proposed antioxidant mechanism is direct radical scavenging by the catechol group, converting carnosic acid into carnosol, together with indirect effects through Nrf2 activation by modification of Keap1 cysteines [3]. Laboratory work in 2025 reported that carnosic acid directly targets the C-terminal tail of STING to dampen STING-driven inflammation in disease models [5]. A 2023 study reported suppression of neutrophil extracellular trap formation in alcoholic hepatosteatosis through a P2X7R-NLRP3 pathway [8].

Preclinical papers cover many tissues. In muscle cells and adipocytes, carnosic acid attenuated free fatty acid-induced insulin resistance [4]. In a neuronal cell model it attenuated amyloid oligomer-induced apoptosis and synaptic impairment [9]. A review of rosemary and its constituents for nervous system disorders describes antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective actions in preclinical work and clinical effects on mood and memory for extracts [10]. A review of anti-ageing natural products lists carnosic acid among the compounds reported to have anti-ageing effects [11]. Grokipedia mentions a 2025 study of a prodrug of carnosic acid that improved memory measures in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease [3].

Safety data are mostly preclinical: Grokipedia reports low acute oral toxicity in rodents (LD50 above 2,000 mg/kg), no reported genotoxicity in available preclinical work, and oral bioavailability estimated below 10 percent [3].

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in 40 healthy volunteers tested a sage extract rich in phenolic diterpenes, including carnosic acid, using the UV erythema test, in which test areas on the back were irradiated with UV light and skin redness was assessed [2]. The study describes the compounds as having antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in vitro and examined whether the extract affected UV-induced redness in people [2].
Other human research on carnosic acid itself is not found; the remaining studies are laboratory or animal work [4][5][8][9].

In the European Union, rosemary extracts standardised to carnosic acid are approved as food additive E392 with category-specific maximum levels, and in the United States rosemary extracts are listed as generally recognised as safe, according to Grokipedia [3]. As with plant extracts generally, topical sensitivity reactions are possible.

lore.intro: Carnosic acid is discussed mainly in supplement, longevity and skincare circles as a rosemary-derived antioxidant; strength-training forums list it in liver-support and antioxidant stacks [12].

claims.claim: Carnosic acid protects skin from UV damage.
claims.believers: Rosemary-extract skincare brands and enthusiasts cite its antioxidant activity and its presence in cosmetic sunscreens [3].
claims.experts: A randomized trial in 40 volunteers tested a sage extract rich in carnosic acid and carnosol against UV-induced redness [2]; Grokipedia notes no clinical photoprotection trials of the pure compound [3].

claims.claim: It is a natural preservative that keeps products from spoiling.
claims.believers: Natural-product makers use rosemary extract in place of synthetic preservatives [1].
claims.experts: It is approved as food additive E392 in the EU and Wikipedia describes use in food and non-food products [1][3].

claims.believers: A strength-training forum thread lists carnosic acid among phase II liver support nutrients [12].
claims.experts: A 2023 laboratory study reported suppression of neutrophil trap formation in alcoholic hepatosteatosis models [8]; no human trial is reported.

claims.believers: Longevity discussions include it among antioxidant compounds [11].
claims.experts: A review lists carnosic acid among natural products reported to have anti-ageing effects in preclinical work [11].
Grokipedia cites a 2025 review linking carnosic acid to dermal papilla cell proliferation [3]; no human hair trial is cited.

claims.believers: Supplement enthusiasts cite its metabolic effects in cell studies.
claims.experts: A 2022 study showed attenuation of free fatty acid-induced insulin resistance in muscle cells and adipocytes [4]; human trials are not reported.
